questions.q: Why does a serving benchmark report p99 latency separately from p50 (median) latency?
options: p99 is always identical to p50 in practice, so it's just a sanity check
A deployment can have a great median while still failing a meaningful fraction of users during traffic spikes, which only the tail reveals
p50 is only used for training, not serving
Reporting both is a vLLM-specific requirement with no practical reason
questions.explain: SLOs are written against percentiles like p99 precisely because a good median can hide a bad tail that real users experience during bursts of traffic.

questions.q: What does TPOT (time-per-output-token) measure, as distinct from TTFT?
options: The total time to load the model into GPU memory
The pace of token generation once the response has already started streaming, as opposed to the wait before it starts
The time to tokenize the input prompt only
The total number of tokens the model can hold in context
questions.explain: TTFT measures the wait before streaming starts; TPOT measures how fast tokens arrive once streaming is underway — two different user-felt experiences.

questions.q: In the illustrative benchmark, the baseline's p50 TTFT looked fine but p99 TTFT missed the target under load. What does that specific pattern point to?
options: The model itself is too large and must be replaced with a smaller one
Queuing under burst traffic — a capacity problem, not a slow model
A bug in the curl smoke test from the previous lesson
The GPU driver is outdated
questions.explain: A good median with a bad tail points at requests queuing during bursts rather than the model being inherently slow, which is a capacity/batching fix rather than a quality or model-size fix.

questions.q: Why is it important to change only one variable per benchmarking run during the tuning loop?
options: vLLM technically only accepts one flag change at a time
Changing multiple variables in the same run makes it impossible to tell which change caused which result
It saves disk space
It is required by the model's license
questions.explain: Isolating one variable per run is what makes the before/after comparison trustworthy — with two simultaneous changes, you can't attribute the improvement (or regression) to either one specifically.

questions.q: What is `vllm bench serve` used for in this capstone?
options: Compiling CUDA kernels for the model
vLLM's built-in subcommand for running online-serving load benchmarks and reporting throughput, TTFT, TPOT, and latency percentiles
Converting the model to a quantized checkpoint
Managing Kubernetes autoscaling policies
questions.explain: vllm bench serve fires synthetic traffic at a running vLLM server and reports the serving metrics that matter — throughput, TTFT, TPOT, and latency percentiles.
